title: Normalising a Density and Reading an Interval
quickIdea: Every density carries an unknown constant until you impose total probability 1; fix the constant first, then integrate over the interval the question asks about.
remember: A PDF must satisfy two conditions: f(x) >= 0 everywhere, and the integral of f over the whole real line equals 1. The second condition alone fixes any unknown constant.
A probability is an integral of the density over an interval, P(a <= X <= b) = F(b) - F(a), not the height of the density at a point.
A density may exceed 1: the uniform density on (0, 0.5) is 2. A probability may not, so any computed probability outside [0, 1] is a signal that the constant was never fixed.
For a discrete variable the same normalisation appears as a sum: the probabilities of all values must add to 1, which is how a missing table entry is found.

Support matters: integrate only over the part of the interval where the density is positive. For the 2025 question the density is zero outside [1, 4], so the limits are 1 and 4 for the constant and 2 and 3 for the probability.
Two quick sanity checks cost seconds: the total must be 1, and the answer must lie between 0 and 1.

example.prompt: The density of X is C x^2 for 1 <= x <= 4 and 0 elsewhere. Find C, then P(2 <= x <= 3).
example.work: Normalise: the integral of C x^2 from 1 to 4 is C [x^3/3] from 1 to 4 = C (64 - 1)/3 = 21C, so C = 1/21. Then P(2 <= x <= 3) = (1/21) [x^3/3] from 2 to 3 = (1/21)(27 - 8)/3 = 19/63.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 Q.48 is this exact computation, and its stated trap is the one to memorise: integrating x^2 from 2 to 3 without the constant gives 19/3, a 'probability' of 6.33. Any answer above 1 means the normalisation step was skipped.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 Q.48: P(x) = C x^2 for 1 <= x <= 4 and 0 otherwise. The probability that x lies between 2 and 3 is ______ (three decimal places).
variations.why: C = 1/21 from the normalisation, then the interval integral gives 19/63. The official key accepts 0.300 to 0.302, and the range exists because of rounding at the third decimal.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: The density of X is k x for 0 <= x <= 2 and 0 elsewhere. Find k and P(X > 1).
variations.why: The integral of kx from 0 to 2 is 2k, so k = 1/2. Then P(X > 1) = the integral of x/2 from 1 to 2 = (4 - 1)/4 = 0.75. The density at x = 2 is 1, which is a height, not a probability.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: The density of X is C(1 + x) for 0 <= x <= 1. Find C and P(X <= 1/2).
variations.why: The integral of C(1+x) from 0 to 1 is C(1 + 1/2) = 3C/2, so C = 2/3. Then P(X <= 1/2) = (2/3)[x + x^2/2] from 0 to 1/2 = (2/3)(1/2 + 1/8) = (2/3)(5/8) = 5/12. The variation replaces a pure power by a shifted one, so the normalising integral is no longer a single term.

trap.what: Integrating over the asked interval without first fixing the constant, or integrating over the wrong limits.
trap.why: The constant is what makes the object a density at all; without it every number computed from it is meaningless. And the limits of the normalising integral are the support, not the interval asked about.
trap.counterexample: Skipping the constant in the 2025 question gives 19/3 = 6.33, which is larger than 1 and so cannot be a probability. Using the limits 0 to 4 instead of 1 to 4 gives C = 3/64 and a final answer of 0.148 instead of 0.302.

check.question: The density of X is 1/(b - a) on (a, b). What is P(X > (a + b)/2)?
check.explanation: The upper half of the interval has length (b - a)/2, and the density is constant, so the probability is ((b - a)/2)/(b - a) = 1/2. That is the uniform distribution, whose mean is the midpoint - so exactly half the mass lies above the mean.
